message.content:
The number you’re looking for is the **Shannon number** – an estimate of how many distinct legal positions can arise in a game of chess.  It’s usually quoted as

\[
\text{Shannon number} \;\approx\; 10^{43}
\]

That means there are on the order of **one hundred thousand trillion trillion trillion** different ways the 32 pieces can be arranged on the 64‑square board while still respecting the rules (e.g., no two kings in check, correct piece counts, etc.).

A few related figures:

| Quantity | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| **All legal positions** | \( \sim 10^{43}\) |
| **All possible positions (legal + illegal)** | \( \sim 10^{47}\) |
| **All possible games (sequences of moves)** | \( \sim 10^{120}\) |

So, if you’re asking “how many different board arrangements can exist in a chess game?” the answer is roughly **\(10^{43}\)**.
